🧵 LLMs are powerful, but generating tokens one-by-one is painfully slow.

A new paper, “Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion,” proposes Uno - a way to make autoregressive LLMs generate multiple tokens in parallel without changing the original model’s output distribution.

Here’s the idea 👇

1/ The problem

Standard LLMs are autoregressive (AR):

“The capital of France is”

→ “Paris”
→ next token
→ next token
→ next token...
Each token depends on the previous one, so generation is inherently sequential.
This becomes expensive for:
• long reasoning traces
• coding agents
• tool-using agents
• RL rollouts
• high-concurrency serving
The GPU often spends more time moving model weights/KV-cache data than doing useful computation.

2/ Speculative decoding helps - but has a cost

Traditional speculative decoding uses:
Small draft model → proposes tokens → large model verifies them
For example:
Draft model proposes:
“The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris”
The large model verifies the proposed sequence in parallel.

If the tokens are accepted, we get several tokens for roughly the cost of one verification step.

The catch?

You need a separate draft model, additional memory, another KV cache, and careful alignment between draft and target models.

3/ Uno asks a different question

What if we could make the same LLM act as both:

🧠 Verifier: original autoregressive model
⚡ Drafter: diffusion-based parallel generator

Instead of training a second draft model, Uno adds lightweight LoRA diffusion adapters to the existing LLM.

So the architecture becomes:

AR weights
→ preserve model quality

Diffusion weights
→ optimize generation speed

The two pathways share the same underlying model.

4/ How does the diffusion pathway work?

Imagine the model has already generated:

“The Eiffel Tower is”
Instead of predicting only:

“located”

the diffusion pathway tries to draft a whole block:

“located in Paris, France.”
These tokens are proposed in parallel.

The goal isn't for the diffusion model to be perfect.
It just needs to produce drafts that are close enough to what the AR model would generate.

5/ The clever part: AR verification

Uno then sends the draft through the original AR model.

Suppose the diffusion pathway proposes:

“located in Paris, France and was completed”

The AR verifier might accept:

“located in Paris, France”

and reject the rest.

Only the valid prefix is retained.

If something is rejected, the AR model samples the correct replacement.

This is why the authors call the acceleration lossless.

The original AR model remains the final authority.

6/ Ψ-Spec

The paper introduces Ψ-Spec, the sampler that combines:

Diffusion drafting + AR verification + rejection sampling

The diffusion model proposes multiple tokens simultaneously.

The AR model verifies them.

Because the verifier is still the original AR model, the sampling procedure preserves its target distribution.

7/ A simple example

Suppose the AR model would generate:

“Machine learning models learn patterns from data.”

Normally:

Step 1: Machine
Step 2: learning
Step 3: models
Step 4: learn
Step 5: patterns
...

Uno might draft:

“Machine learning models learn patterns”

in parallel.

The verifier checks the proposed tokens.

If all are valid, several tokens are emitted in one iteration.

So instead of:

1 token → verify → 1 token → verify → 1 token

we get:

multiple-token draft → verify → multiple accepted tokens

That is where the speedup comes from.

8/ Why LoRA?
The diffusion pathway uses lightweight LoRA adapters rather than another full model.
For the Qwen3-8B experiment, the adapters add only about 0.35B trainable parameters.
This is significantly smaller than the 1.05B-parameter DFlash drafter used as one of the baselines.

Uno also shares a KV cache between drafting and verification, reducing peak memory.
9/ Training is also interesting
The authors don't retrain the whole LLM.

They first train the normal AR model.

Then:

Freeze the AR weights

Add diffusion LoRA adapters

Corrupt token blocks using discrete diffusion

Train the adapters to reconstruct/draft the tokens

Encourage drafts that have high acceptance probability under the AR verifier

The paper uses Diffusion Consistency Distillation + Total Variation loss for this process.

10/ Why this matters

The diffusion adapters are essentially learning:

“How can I predict several tokens at once that the original AR model is likely to accept?”

So the expensive model doesn't need to change its behavior.

The additional parameters are dedicated almost entirely to making inference faster.

That separation of quality vs. speed is the core design idea.

11/ The results are impressive
For the Qwen-based UnoQwen model:

⚡ 5,733 tokens/sec system throughput

vs.

• EAGLE-3: 4,944 tok/s
• DFlash: 5,351 tok/s

At maximum batch size, UnoQwen reaches about 1.6× the throughput of the base AR model.
At batch size 1, it reaches about 2.5× speedup over the base model.
12/ It isn't just about batch size 1
This is an important point in the paper.
Many acceleration papers emphasize single-request latency.

But real-world agentic systems often have:

• multiple users
• parallel agents
• tool calls
• retries
• branching trajectories
• RL rollouts

So the authors measure both:

Per-request throughput

and

System throughput at high batch sizes.

Uno maintains its speed advantage across evaluated batch sizes.

13/ Uno vs diffusion LLMs

Conventional diffusion LLMs can generate tokens in parallel, but they often introduce a quality ↔ speed tradeoff because the underlying AR model is modified or replaced.

Uno takes a different approach:

AR model = quality

Diffusion adapter = speed
AR verifier = correctness

So the diffusion component doesn't have to become the final model.

It only needs to produce useful proposals.

14/ Uno can also accelerate RL

This may be one of the most practical applications.

RL training for LLMs requires huge numbers of rollouts.

If generation is faster, RL training becomes faster too.

The paper reports up to 40% end-to-end RL training speedup, particularly for mathematics and coding experts.

15/ The broader idea
The interesting conceptual takeaway isn't just “diffusion makes LLMs faster.”
It's:
Separate the model that defines the distribution from the mechanism used to sample from it efficiently.
The AR model defines:

“What should the model generate?”

The diffusion pathway learns:

“How can we propose several tokens at once?”

The verifier guarantees:

“Only outputs consistent with the AR distribution survive.”

16/ Why I think this is interesting

There are three different approaches to faster LLM inference:

Speculative decoding

→ separate draft model

Diffusion LLMs

→ parallel generation, but potentially lossy

Uno

→ diffusion-based drafting + original AR verification

The third approach tries to combine the best properties of both.

17/ The key numbers

📌 UnoQwen
• 8B base model
• +0.35B diffusion parameters
• ~5,733 tok/s system throughput
• ~1.6× faster than base AR at max batch
• ~2.5× faster at batch size 1
• lower peak memory than EAGLE-3/DFlash

And the full Uno model reports speedups of up to ~3×, with gains retained at high batch sizes.

18/ The one-sentence summary

Uno turns diffusion into a lightweight “parallel proposal engine” for an autoregressive LLM, while keeping the original AR model as the exact verifier.

That gives you:

⚡ parallel token generation
🧠 original model quality
✅ lossless verification
💾 fewer additional parameters
📈 better throughput
🚀 faster RL rollouts

This is a pretty compelling direction for making long-context and agentic LLM workloads cheaper and faster.

Generative Art was here befoe AI: 
Before computers. The idea starts as instruction plus chance.Mozart-era musical dice games let rules assemble minuets. Dada and Cage used chance operations so the artist would not control every event. Sol LeWitt’s wall drawings made the score the work: written rules, executed by other hands. Constructivism and Op art trained people to think in systems, grids, and variation. Jacquard looms and Ada Lovelace’s 1843 notes on Babbage already implied that a machine following a procedure could do more than calculate — it could compose. 

https://t.co/dzNa0FkX6w

That is the prehistory: the artist writes conditions; something else completes the picture.1960s: plotters and the AlgoristsThe first public computer-art shows happen in 1965.Georg Nees exhibits plotter drawings in Stuttgart in February 1965. Frieder Nake follows. In New York, A. Michael Noll and Béla Julesz show computer-generated pictures at Howard Wise Gallery. Noll had started deliberately making “computer art” at Bell Labs in 1962 after a plotter bug produced a mess someone joked was art. He then programmed order plus disorder on purpose. 

https://t.co/Uwx4OQ3ZpJ

Nees’s Schotter (Gravel) is the textbook image of that idea: a grid of squares that begins regular and tilts into chaos as it descends. The work is not “the computer drew a picture.” It is a rule about how much disorder to https://t.co/0AC8vq4Qc8

Vera Molnár is the other pillar. In Paris she invented a machine imaginaire — executing algorithms by hand — before she got mainframe access in 1968. Then FORTRAN, BASIC, plotters. Grids, letters, controlled percentages of disorder. She came from painting and Constructivism, not from a lab demo. 

https://t.co/XYpbjyWDpz

https://t.co/v1g9yyoV32

Around them: Manfred Mohr, Charles Csuri (Sine Curve Man, 1967), Hiroshi Kawano, Herbert Franke, Lillian Schwartz, John and James Whitney in film. Jean-Pierre Hébert later named this loose family the Algorists: artists who write algorithms as their medium. 

https://t.co/GZAtxx872N

1968: the public discovers the fieldJasia Reichardt’s Cybernetic Serendipity at London’s ICA (2 August–20 October 1968) is the first big international survey of computers and the arts. Graphics, films, generated music, robots, cybernetic sculptures. Artists, engineers, and composers in one room. Tens of thousands of visitors. It tours to Washington and San Francisco. Harold Cohen later said seeing that show helped push him toward machine art. 

https://t.co/pssQ14IIuz

MoMA’s The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age (also 1968) and later Software at the Jewish Museum (1970) keep the argument inside institutions: is the program the work, or the print it leaves behind? 

https://t.co/XYpbjyWDpz

Cohen and AARON: the long AI projectHarold Cohen, already a painter who had represented Britain at Venice, starts AARON in the early 1970s after time at Stanford’s AI Lab. It is not a prompt box. It is a drawing program he rewrites for decades: first abstract marks, then plants and figures, then color. AARON draws; Cohen designs what AARON is allowed to know about composition, closure, and form. Museums let it work in public at SFMOMA and the Tate. That is still the cleanest historical example of an artist building a collaborator instead of renting a generator. 

https://t.co/t30TGbBoaF

https://t.co/ADGTFNhWV6

https://t.co/FoDccQZBNP

1980s–1990s: fractals, scenes, closed shopsMandelbrot’s fractals leak into popular “computer art.” Plotter and algorithmic artists keep working with less fashion heat. The demoscene treats realtime code as craft. John Maeda’s Design By Numbers at MIT tries to give visual people a programming language small enough to sketch with. Flash becomes a mass tool for motion systems. The through-line is the same: code as pencil, not code as vending machine.2001: ProcessingCasey Reas and Ben Fry release Processing, built out of Maeda’s MIT orbit. Goal: artists and designers write systems the way they used to sketch. Reas’s own Process series is explicit LeWitt-into-software: rules for elements and behaviors, then the program runs. Jared Tarbell, Marius Watz, and a generation of “creative coders” come out of that stack. Open source matters here. The tool is inspectable. The system can be shown, not only the JPEG. 

https://t.co/ADGTFNhWV6

2014–2018: GANs become “the look”Ian Goodfellow’s generative adversarial networks (2014) give artists a new engine: a generator tries to fool a discriminator trained on a dataset. Mario Klingemann, Helena Sarin, and others treat the network as a material you tune — datasets, thresholds, failure modes. Refik Anadol scales data-trained “hallucinations” into museums. 

https://t.co/KdiRsEww0Z

The market event is Obvious’s Portrait of Edmond de Belamy at Christie’s in 2018: $432,500. A blurry invented aristocrat, signed with a GAN formula. It made “AI art” a headline and also a fight. Many working GAN artists pointed out that Obvious used an existing model and training approach; the auction sold the idea of machine authorship more than a deep studio practice. That split — spectacle versus built system — never went away. 

https://t.co/M9cFVWkrci

What is PPO vs DPO vs GRPO? (in AI engineer interviews)

Let's learn together ↓

These are three different recipes for aligning LLMs with human preferences.

They all try to make a model produce better outputs. But they disagree on how to measure "better" and what machinery you need to get there.

The tradeoff is always the same: more control vs. less memory vs. fewer assumptions.

The formulas:

PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization):
L_CLIP = E[ min(r_t × A_t, clip(r_t, 1-ε, 1+ε) × A_t) ]

Where:
r_t → ratio of new policy to old policy (π_θ / π_old)
A_t → advantage estimate from value network
ε → clipping range, keeps updates inside a trust region

DPO (Direct Preference Optimization):
L_DPO = -log σ(β log π_θ(y_w)/π_ref(y_w) - β log π_θ(y_l)/π_ref(y_l))

Where:
y_w → the preferred (winning) response
y_l → the rejected (losing) response
β → controls how sharp the gradient signal is
π_ref → frozen reference policy (SFT model)

GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization):
Â_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r), where r = {r_1, ..., r_G}

Where:
r_i → reward for the i-th output in the group
G → number of sampled outputs per prompt
Â_i → z-scored advantage, replaces the value network

How each one works:

PPO:
1. Sample a response from the current policy
2. Score it with a learned reward model, subtract KL penalty
3. Estimate advantages using a value network (GAE)
4. Update policy with clipped objective, stay near old policy

DPO:
1. Collect static preference pairs (prompt, y_w, y_l)
2. Keep a frozen reference policy
3. Compute log-ratio differences for both responses
4. Minimize the log-sigmoid loss directly, no reward model needed

GRPO:
1. For each prompt, sample G outputs from the policy
2. Score each with a reward model
3. Z-score the rewards across the group to get advantages
4. Run a PPO-style update, no value network required

🧐 How do they actually differ?

Memory cost:
PPO needs 4 models (policy, ref, reward, value). DPO needs 2 (policy, ref). GRPO sits in between at 2-3.

Data requirement:
PPO and GRPO need online rollouts. DPO works offline with pre-collected pairs, no sampling budget needed.

Reward type:
PPO uses a learned reward model. DPO bakes the reward signal into the loss implicitly. GRPO expects verifiable rewards (math answers, code tests, format checks).

Baseline:
PPO uses a value network to reduce variance. GRPO replaces that with group z-scoring. DPO skips the baseline problem entirely.

When to use each:
PPO when you have a dense reward signal and token-level credit assignment matters. DPO when you have static preference pairs and no online sampling budget. GRPO when rewards are verifiable (math, code, format) and running many rollouts per prompt is cheap.

And even if a senior engineer chooses to use an LLM to increase their output, who are we to judge their morality?

Is it legal? Yes.

Then it's none of our business.

Would we buy a fully AI-generated game or movie? Hell no! I'll vote with my wallet.

At the end of the day, everyone makes plenty of morally questionable choices. Some people eat meat, some support fast fashion, and others support big tech corporations by buying fancy hardware.

Morality is a spectrum, and we should respect each other's choices.
